title: Index of the Largest Element
statement:
Find where the largest value in an array lives, not what it is.

## Your procedure

```
int index_of_max(const int *values, int count);
```

Return the index of the largest element. If the largest value appears more
than once, return the index of the **first** one. If `count` is `0`, return
`-1`.

## The calling convention

Microsoft x64. The first four integer or pointer arguments arrive in
registers, and a 32-bit result goes back in `eax`:

| | 1st | 2nd | 3rd | 4th | return |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 64-bit | `rcx` | `rdx` | `r8` | `r9` | `rax` |
| 32-bit | `ecx` | `edx` | `r8d` | `r9d` | `eax` |

`rax`, `rcx`, `rdx`, `r8`-`r11` are yours to clobber. `rbx`, `rbp`, `rsi`,
`rdi` and `r12`-`r15` belong to the caller: use one and you must `push` it on
the way in and `pop` it on the way out.

Nothing here needs the stack, so nothing here needs a prologue.

## Watch out

- Two things have to be carried through the loop, not one: the best value
  seen so far *and* where it was. Registers are cheap -- use two.
- "First one wins" on a tie is decided by the comparison you branch on.
  Replacing the current best only when the new value is *strictly* greater
  keeps the earlier index; replacing on greater-or-equal quietly returns the
  last one instead.
- The values are signed, so compare with `jg`/`jle`, not `ja`/`jbe`. The
  unsigned conditions read `-1` as roughly four billion and will happily
  call it the largest element in the array.
- `count == 0` returns `-1` and must not load anything. `values` may be null.
starter_code:
; int index_of_max(const int *values, int count)
;
;   rcx = values (the array)
;   edx = count  (how many elements)
;   eax = the index you return, or -1 for an empty array

.code
index_of_max PROC
    ; your code here
    mov eax, -1
    ret
index_of_max ENDP
end

tests.name: empty array
tests.description: Return -1 without loading through a null pointer.

tests.name: largest is first
tests.description: Nothing after the first element beats it, so the index must stay put.

tests.name: tie keeps the earlier index
tests.description: Both 7s are the largest. Replacing on >= instead of > returns 3 here.

tests.name: all negative
tests.description: An unsigned comparison reads -9 as the largest and answers 0.
